description: Alkylating agents, whether environmental or endogenous, leave methyl adducts such as 1-methyladenine and 3-methylcytosine on DNA bases, where they block base pairing and stall replication. ALKBH2-mediated reversal of alkylation damage erases these lesions directly, without excising the base or breaking the backbone, so no repair patch or strand gap is ever created. ALKBH2 is an iron(II)- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase, a human counterpart of bacterial AlkB, that hydroxylates the offending methyl group; the unstable intermediate collapses and releases formaldehyde, regenerating the unmodified base. Longer adducts such as 1-ethyladenine are removed the same way, yielding acetaldehyde. Acting mainly on double-stranded DNA and enriched at replication foci, this repair route protects genome integrity and shapes cellular sensitivity to alkylating chemotherapy.

Abasic sites arise constantly in DNA, both spontaneously and as intermediates left behind by glycosylases that excise damaged bases, and they must be cleaned up before replication turns them into mutations or strand breaks. This branch of base excision repair resolves them without the usual AP endonuclease step: NEIL1 and NEIL2, bifunctional glycosylases with beta/delta lyase activity, incise the strand and leave a 3' phosphate and a 5' deoxyribose phosphate. DNA polymerase beta trims the 5'dRP but is blocked by the 3' phosphate, so the phosphatase activity of PNKP must restore a 3'-hydroxyl before a single replacement nucleotide can be inserted and the nick sealed by the XRCC1-scaffolded LIG3 complex. The route matters for handling oxidative lesions, including those generated by OGG1, and for limiting mutagenesis in transcribed and replicating DNA.

The first committed step of base excision repair is removal of a chemically damaged purine base from DNA, and this is where that cleavage happens: DNA glycosylases hydrolyse the N-glycosidic bond, releasing the damaged base and leaving an abasic site for downstream endonuclease, polymerase and ligase steps. It matters because oxidation and alkylation of guanine and adenine are constant products of respiration and environmental exposure, and unrepaired 8-oxoguanine mispairs with adenine to fix G:C to T:A transversions. OGG1 excises 8-oxoguanine, MUTYH removes the adenine misinserted opposite it, MPG handles alkylated and deaminated purines, and NEIL3 acts on further oxidised lesions. Histones place the reaction in chromatin, while the shelterin components mark telomeric DNA as a distinct substrate. Loss of MUTYH causes an inherited polyposis and colorectal cancer predisposition.

When a replication fork meets a UV-induced thymine dimer, the replicative polymerase stalls; DNA polymerase eta rescues it by copying directly across the lesion, inserting two adenines opposite the dimer with high fidelity. This translesion synthesis route is what keeps sunlight-damaged skin cells replicating accurately, and losing it causes the variant form of xeroderma pigmentosum, in which patients are extremely photosensitive and develop skin cancers early because the damage is bypassed by error-prone polymerases instead. Single-stranded DNA at the stalled fork is coated by the RPA complex, the clamp loader RFC loads PCNA, and monoubiquitinated PCNA recruits polymerase eta through its ubiquitin-binding domain. After a few nucleotides are added, the enzyme must be removed and the replicative polymerase restored: SPRTN and the VCP/p97 segregase with its UFD1-NPLOC4 cofactors, together with ubiquitin supplied by the polyubiquitin genes, drive that exchange.

Oxidation and deamination constantly damage the pyrimidine bases of DNA, and the first committed step of base excision repair is removal of the damaged base by a glycosylase that recognises it. Cleavage of the damaged pyrimidine is carried out here by uracil DNA glycosylases UNG and SMUG1, the thymine and mismatch glycosylases TDG and MBD4, and the oxidised-pyrimidine enzymes NTHL1 and the NEIL family, which hydrolyse the N-glycosidic bond to leave an abasic site for downstream incision, gap filling and ligation. Without this step, deaminated cytosine and oxidised bases are read as mutations, driving C-to-T transitions and cancer predisposition. The presence of histones and of shelterin components such as TERF1, TERF2, POT1 and TINF2 reflects that this chemistry operates on nucleosomal DNA and is needed at telomeres, where guanine and pyrimidine oxidation threatens chromosome-end integrity.

Global genome nucleotide excision repair removes bulky, helix-distorting lesions such as UV photoproducts and chemical adducts from anywhere in the genome, and the dual incision step is the committed cut that releases them. Once the damage-verification factors XPA, RPA and the TFIIH helicases ERCC2/ERCC3 have opened a bubble around the lesion, the ERCC1-ERCC4 endonuclease cuts 5' to the damage and ERCC5 cuts 3', excising a roughly 27-30 nucleotide fragment. The resulting gap is immediately filled, so replication factor C, PCNA and DNA polymerases delta, epsilon and kappa are recruited as part of the same transaction. Damage recognition by the DDB1-DDB2 complex with cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase components, plus PARP1/PARP2, marks lesions in chromatin for this processing. Loss of these incision activities underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sun sensitivity and skin cancer predisposition.

Repair of a double-strand break by homologous recombination requires a search for an intact sister template, and this presynaptic step builds the tool that performs the search. Resection nucleases and helicases acting with the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex and CtIP generate long 3' single-stranded tails, which RPA coats to remove secondary structure. BRCA2, working with BRCA1-BARD1 and licensed by checkpoint kinase signalling through ATM, ATR and CHEK1, then loads RAD51 onto that ssDNA in place of RPA, nucleating the helical nucleoprotein filament that will invade duplex DNA. Paralogue complexes containing RAD51B, RAD51C, RAD51D and XRCC2 stabilise the filament. The same events sustain the damage checkpoint via the 9-1-1 clamp and its loader. Loss of these factors causes error-prone repair, chromosomal instability and hereditary breast, ovarian and Fanconi-type cancer predisposition, and underlies sensitivity to PARP inhibition.

Base excision repair begins when a DNA glycosylase recognises a damaged or mismatched base and cuts it out, leaving an abasic site. These glycosylases bind their product tightly, so the abasic site must be handed off rather than simply released, and this step is that handoff: the AP endonuclease APEX1 displaces the bound glycosylase and takes possession of the lesion before cleaving the backbone for downstream repair synthesis. The arrangement protects the cell from the abasic site itself, which is mutagenic and blocks replication if left exposed. The glycosylases involved cover the common chemistries of DNA damage "" oxidised guanine and thymine, alkylated purines, uracil from cytosine deamination or misincorporation, and mismatches opposite oxidised bases "" and inherited defects in this repair route, such as MUTYH deficiency, predispose to colorectal adenomas and cancer. The step couples lesion recognition to strand incision and keeps repair intermediates channelled from one enzyme to the next.

Homologous recombination repair of a double-strand break can end without exchanging chromosome arms, and synthesis-dependent strand annealing is the route that achieves it. After the invading strand has been extended using the sister chromatid as template, the extended strand is displaced from the D-loop and reanneals with its original partner, so repair restores sequence without generating a crossover — the outcome that protects cells from loss of heterozygosity and gross rearrangement. Upstream components carry out end resection and filament assembly: the MRE11–RAD50–NBN complex with CtIP, EXO1, DNA2 and the BLM–TOP3A–RMI1–RMI2 dissolvasome, then BRCA1–BARD1, PALB2 and BRCA2 loading RAD51 and its paralogues. The helicase RTEL1 promotes D-loop disassembly, remaining gaps are filled by polymerase-mediated synthesis, and nicks are ligated. Loss of these factors underlies hereditary breast and ovarian cancer predisposition and sensitivity to crosslinking agents.

Microhomology-mediated end joining, also called alternative nonhomologous end joining, is a mutagenic backup route for repairing DNA double-strand breaks that operates when high-fidelity repair is saturated or genetically compromised. It matters clinically because tumours deficient in homologous recombination, such as BRCA-mutant cancers, lean on it to survive, which is why polymerase theta and PARP are drug targets there. Repair begins with limited end resection by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN nuclease complex together with CtIP, generating 3' single-stranded overhangs that are not licensed for recombination. PARP1 or PARP2 and DNA polymerase theta then align the two ends through short microhomologous tracts, POLQ extends by strand-displacement synthesis, FEN1 trims the displaced 5' flaps, and LIG3 with XRCC1 seals the remaining nicks. The outcome is invariably a deletion spanning the sequence between microhomologies, plus frequent base substitutions and occasional chromosomal translocations.

When RNA polymerase II stalls at a bulky, helix-distorting lesion, transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair removes the damaged strand; this final stage refills and seals the resulting single-stranded gap so transcription can resume. Loss of the pathway underlies Cockayne syndrome and UV-sensitive syndrome, where neurons and other non-dividing cells accumulate transcription-blocking damage and degenerate. After dual incision, RPA coats the gap, the clamp loader RFC deposits PCNA, and DNA polymerases delta or epsilon, or the translesion polymerase kappa, synthesize the repair patch; ligase I or ligase III with its partner XRCC1 then seals the nick. The stalled polymerase complex, the CSA and CSB proteins with UVSSA and a cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase, and the TFIIH helicases provide the damage-recognition and unwinding context, linking genome maintenance directly to ongoing gene expression.

Base excision repair removes damaged and abasic bases, and when the 5' end of the resulting nick cannot be trimmed by a simple one-nucleotide patch, the cell switches to long-patch repair using the replication machinery. This PCNA-dependent branch keeps oxidative and alkylation damage from becoming mutations or strand breaks, and it operates most readily in S phase, when replication factors are abundant. After the AP endonuclease APEX1 incises the abasic site, DNA polymerase beta adds the first nucleotide and displaces the intractable 5' abasic sugar phosphate; the clamp loader RFC loads PCNA, and polymerase delta or epsilon extends strand-displacement synthesis with RPA coating the displaced flap. FEN1 excises that flap and DNA ligase I seals the patch. The same clamp, clamp loader and polymerases serve genome replication, so this route links damage repair directly to replicative synthesis.

When a replication fork meets a damaged base it stalls, and translesion synthesis by DNA polymerase kappa is one of the routes that lets replication continue past the lesion rather than collapse. POLK is a Y-family polymerase particularly suited to copying past oxidised bases such as thymine glycol and 8-oxoguanine and past bulky adducts formed by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, so it limits fork breakage and the chromosomal damage that follows, at the cost of introducing mutations. Recruitment depends on monoubiquitinated PCNA, loaded by the replication factor C clamp loader and marked using the ubiquitin pool encoded by UBB, UBC and the ribosomal fusion genes; RPA coats the exposed single strand. POLK acts with REV1 and the REV3L-MAD2L2 polymerase zeta complex, which extends the nucleotide inserted opposite the lesion, making this a damage-tolerance rather than a repair pathway.

Repair of DNA double-strand breaks must be switched off as well as on, and this pathway describes how the break response is damped by destroying the proteins that organize it. The BRCA1-BARD1 heterodimer, which drives homologous recombination and end resection, is polyubiquitinated by Cullin4-RBX1-DDB1 ubiquitin ligase complexes using DCAF8L1 or DCAF8L2 as substrate receptors, and the tagged proteins are then degraded by the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core particle, ATPase and lid subunits is represented here along with ubiquitin itself. Limiting BRCA1-BARD1 levels restrains recombination, influences the choice between repair routes, and tunes how long checkpoint signalling persists after damage. Because BRCA1-BARD1 loss underlies hereditary breast and ovarian cancer, ubiquitin-dependent turnover of these factors also shapes genome stability and the sensitivity of tumour cells to agents that create double-strand breaks.

Bulky, helix-distorting lesions such as UV photoproducts must be found before they can be cut out, and damage recognition in global genome nucleotide excision repair is the search step that scans the entire genome rather than only transcribed strands. Two sensors cooperate: an XPC complex with RAD23A or RAD23B and centrin-2 probes for destabilised base pairing and binds the undamaged strand, while the UV-DDB ubiquitin ligase built on DDB2, DDB1, a cullin-4 scaffold and RBX1 engages the lesion itself and helps retain XPC there. Ubiquitin transfer, modulated by the COP9 signalosome, and PARP1/PARP2 activity mark the site, and INO80 chromatin remodelling opens nucleosomal DNA for access. Loss of these factors underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sun sensitivity and skin cancer, placing this step upstream of the incision and resynthesis stages of repair.

Alkylating agents, whether environmental or endogenous, leave methyl adducts on DNA bases that block base pairing and stall replication. Direct reversal by ALKBH3 erases two of the most damaging of these, 1-methyladenine and 3-methylcytosine, restoring the unmodified base in a single oxidative step rather than excising and resynthesising the strand. The enzyme is an iron(II)- and alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase that hydroxylates the offending methyl group so it falls away as formaldehyde; an ethyl adduct is released as acetaldehyde. Because ALKBH3 works best on single-stranded DNA, repair of duplex substrates requires the ASCC complex, whose ASCC3 helicase unwinds the damaged region while ASCC1 and ASCC2 target the activity to sites of alkylation damage. This chemistry contributes to alkylation tolerance and shapes how tumour cells respond to methylating chemotherapy.

Alkylating agents, whether endogenous metabolites or chemotherapy drugs, can transfer a methyl group to the O6 position of guanine, creating a base that pairs ambiguously with both cytosine and thymine and therefore seeds G:C to A:T transition mutations at the next round of replication. Direct reversal by MGMT removes this lesion before it is copied, restoring guanine in a single step without excising the base or nicking the backbone. The protein accepts the methyl group onto an active-site cysteine and is thereby inactivated, so each molecule acts only once and the cell's capacity is set by how much of it is present. Silencing of the gene by promoter hypermethylation is common in glioma and other tumours, raising mutational load but also sensitising those tumours to alkylating chemotherapy such as temozolomide, which makes this repair route a prognostic and predictive marker in oncology.

When a damaged or mismatched base is excised by a DNA glycosylase, the DNA is left with an abasic site whose sugar-phosphate remnant must be cleared before the gap can be filled; this is the short-patch, single-nucleotide replacement arm of base excision repair. Without it, abasic sites and their 5'-deoxyribose phosphate residues persist as blocking, mutagenic lesions that stall replication and drive base substitutions, which is why this chemistry underlies genome stability against oxidative and alkylation damage. APEX1 displaces the glycosylase from its product and incises the backbone on the 5' side of the base-free deoxyribose, creating a nick with a 3'-hydroxyl. DNA polymerase beta is then recruited to the resulting gap and uses its lyase activity to release the 5'dRP group, leaving a clean single-nucleotide gap for fill-in synthesis and ligation.

A DNA double-strand break must be converted into a signal that stops the cell cycle and marshals repair machinery, and this is the step that builds that signal at the break. The MRN complex (MRE11:RAD50:NBN) senses broken ends and activates ATM, which phosphorylates histone H2AX on serine 139; the resulting gamma-H2AX mark spreads over flanking chromatin and docks MDC1, creating ionizing radiation-induced foci. Ubiquitin ligases RNF8 and RNF168, with HERC2 and ubiquitin conjugating enzymes, modify histones to retain downstream factors, recruiting UIMC1/RAP80 and the BRCA1-A complex, while removal of the KDM4A/KDM4B demethylases and NSD2-dependent H4K20 methylation license 53BP1 binding. ATM then phosphorylates BRCA1:BARD1, 53BP1 and CHEK2, enforcing checkpoint arrest via TP53 and biasing repair toward homologous recombination or end joining. Loss of these components underlies radiosensitivity, immunodeficiency and hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.

Homologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks begins with strand invasion, and the branched D-loop that results must be taken apart before chromosomes can segregate. How it is dismantled determines the genetic outcome: the BLM-TOP3A-RMI1-RMI2 helicase-topoisomerase complex dissolves double Holliday junctions to give non-crossover products and suppresses sister chromatid exchange, while nucleolytic resolvases such as GEN1 and the SLX1A-SLX4 partnership with MUS81-EME1/EME2 cleave them and yield crossovers. Crossovers in mitotic cells risk loss of heterozygosity, exposing recessive mutations in tumour suppressors, so the choice between routes is a genome-stability decision. The upstream context is present too: MRE11-RAD50-NBN and CtIP-driven resection with EXO1 and DNA2, ATM signalling, BRCA1-BARD1 and BRCA2-PALB2 loading of RAD51 with its paralogues, and SPIDR with FIGNL1-FIRRM biasing recombination toward the non-crossover path. Mutation of these factors underlies Bloom syndrome and hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.

A double-strand break is the most dangerous lesion a genome can sustain, and this pathway is the first step by which a cell notices one. The MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex binds the broken ends and holds them together, and its recruitment converts a physical break into a signal: the acetyltransferase KAT5 acetylates ATM, which autophosphorylates and switches from an inactive dimer to an active monomeric kinase. Active ATM then phosphorylates the substrates that arrest the cell cycle and assemble repair factors at the lesion, so detection and the damage response are coupled at their origin. Import of components into the nucleus depends on karyopherin-mediated transport. Loss of this sensing step underlies ataxia-telangiectasia and the related Nijmegen breakage and MRE11-deficiency syndromes, with radiosensitivity, immunodeficiency, chromosomal instability and cancer predisposition.

When RNA polymerase II stalls at a bulky lesion in a transcribed strand, transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair removes the damage so that gene expression can resume; the dual incision step is where the damaged oligonucleotide is actually cut out. Loss of this route causes Cockayne syndrome and UV-sensitive syndrome, with photosensitivity, developmental failure and neurodegeneration rather than the cancer predisposition typical of the global-genome branch. Stalled polymerase must first backtrack to expose the lesion, aided by ERCC6 and ERCC8-dependent remodelling and ubiquitination, UVSSA, TCEA1-stimulated nascent RNA cleavage, and the helicase subunits of TFIIH. The ERCC1:ERCC4 endonuclease then incises 5' of the lesion and ERCC5 3' of it, on a substrate stabilised by XPA and the RPA trimer, leaving a gap that replicative polymerases with PCNA and clamp loader refill.

Translesion synthesis lets a replication fork copy past a damaged base, but the Y-family polymerases that do it are error-prone, so cells must switch back to accurate replication as soon as the lesion is passed. Terminating translesion DNA synthesis is that switch, and its failure raises the mutation burden carried forward into daughter cells, a route toward the mutational signatures seen in tumours. Monoubiquitinated PCNA recruits the bypass polymerases eta, iota, kappa and REV1; removing that ubiquitin mark, by deubiquitinases including USP10, evicts them and restores processive synthesis by polymerases delta and epsilon loaded via replication factor C on RPA-coated template. An ISG15 arm, acting through UBA7, UBE2L6 and TRIM25, modifies PCNA and PCLAF to help disengage the bypass machinery, linking interferon-inducible conjugation to the fidelity of damage tolerance and to normal fork restart.

Base excision repair begins when a DNA glycosylase scans duplex DNA, flips out an aberrant base and prepares it for removal, and this step covers recognition of damaged or mismatched pyrimidines in particular. It is the cell's main defence against the constant chemical erosion of bases by oxidation, deamination and alkylation, and its failure drives point mutation and cancer predisposition, as seen with germline defects in the uracil- and thymine-directed glycosylases. Uracil arising from cytosine deamination or misincorporation is handled by UNG and SMUG1, mismatched thymine at CpG sites by TDG and MBD4, and oxidised pyrimidines by NTHL1 and the NEIL enzymes, while OGG1 addresses oxidised purines. Because lesions must be found within chromatin, core histones and the telomere-binding shelterin proteins are part of the context in which recognition occurs, linking this repair step to nucleosome packaging and telomere maintenance.

Double-strand breaks are the most dangerous lesions a genome can suffer, and nonhomologous end joining is the route that repairs them by re-ligating the two ends directly, without a homologous template. It works throughout the cell cycle, dominates in G1, and is the mechanism that seals the programmed breaks of antigen receptor gene rearrangement — loss of its ligase or nuclease components causes radiosensitivity and severe combined immunodeficiency. Break recognition by the MRE11–RAD50–NBN complex activates ATM, which phosphorylates H2AX; ubiquitin signalling through RNF8, RNF168 and UBE2N builds the foci that recruit 53BP1 with RIF1 and PAXIP1, blocking end resection and steering repair away from homologous recombination. The Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer with DNA-PKcs synapses the ends, ARTEMIS trims overhangs, TDP1 and TDP2 clear blocking adducts, polymerases mu and lambda fill short gaps, and XRCC4–LIG4 with XLF completes ligation, sometimes with small deletions.

Bulky helix-distorting DNA lesions such as UV photoproducts are removed anywhere in the genome by global genome nucleotide excision repair, and this step builds the machinery that actually cuts them out. Once damage-sensing proteins XPC with its partners and the UV-DDB complex mark the site, the transcription factor TFIIH is recruited; its helicase subunits ERCC2 and ERCC3 open a bubble around the lesion while XPA verifies that real damage is present and RPA coats the undamaged strand to shield it. The endonucleases ERCC5 and the ERCC1-ERCC4 heterodimer then dock to form the incision complex that excises the damaged oligonucleotide. Assembly is tuned by PARP1/PARP2, ubiquitin ligase activity of CUL4-DDB1-RBX1, and SUMO conjugation with SUMO-targeted ubiquitylation. Loss of these factors underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sunlight sensitivity and skin cancer predisposition.

Base excision repair removes damaged or inappropriate bases, and when the resulting gap cannot be sealed after a single nucleotide is added, the cell switches to a long-patch route that displaces and trims a short flap before ligation. This variant keeps oxidative and alkylation damage from persisting as single-strand breaks, which otherwise collapse replication forks and drive mutation and genome instability. After APEX1 incises the abasic site, DNA polymerase beta performs strand-displacement synthesis of roughly two to ten nucleotides; FEN1 cleaves the displaced flap and DNA ligase I seals the nick. PARP1 and PARP2 detect the break and synthesise poly(ADP-ribose) to recruit and coordinate these factors, while PARG and ADPRS reverse that modification so the repair machinery can be released. The same damage-sensing step is what PARP inhibitors exploit therapeutically.

Before a broken chromosome can be repaired using a sister chromatid as template, the two DNA ends must be trimmed back to leave long single-stranded 3' tails, and this end-processing step is what commits a double-strand break to homology-directed repair rather than to blunt-end joining. Resection proceeds in two stages: the MRE11-RAD50-NBN nuclease complex with CtIP and BRCA1-BARD1 initiates trimming, then EXO1 or DNA2 working with the BLM or WRN helicases extends it over kilobases. CDK2-cyclin A activity restricts initiation to S and G2 phases when a sister chromatid exists, while ATM-dependent phosphorylation and ubiquitin and SUMO marks laid on chromatin histones by RNF8, RNF168 and associated ligases organise factor recruitment around the break. RPA-coated overhangs then recruit ATR-ATRIP with TOPBP1, RAD17-RFC and the RAD9-HUS1-RAD1 clamp to activate CHEK1 checkpoint signalling. Loss of these steps underlies chromosomal instability and hereditary breast and ovarian cancer predisposition.

When RNA polymerase II stalls at a lesion in the transcribed strand, cells assemble the pre-incision complex of transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair, the step that verifies the damage and opens the DNA before cutting. This route clears bulky, transcription-blocking lesions from active genes, and its loss causes Cockayne syndrome and UV-sensitive syndrome, with premature ageing, neurodegeneration and failure to resume transcription after UV rather than cancer predisposition. ERCC6 (CSB) recognises the stalled polymerase and brings in ERCC8 (CSA) within a CUL4A/CUL4B-DDB1-RBX1 ubiquitin ligase regulated by the COP9 signalosome; UVSSA delivers the deubiquitinase USP7 to protect ERCC6 from degradation. XPA arrives with the ten-subunit TFIIH complex, whose ERCC2 and ERCC3 helicases unwind the damaged duplex, while the XAB2 complex and the elongation factor TCEA1 help the polymerase backtrack so repair proteins can reach the lesion.

Interstrand crosslinks covalently tie the two strands of the double helix together and block both replication and transcription until they are removed. This route unhooks certain crosslinks directly, using the DNA glycosylase NEIL3 to cleave one of the two glycosidic bonds holding the lesion in place, converting the crosslink into a pair of more tractable single-strand lesions that base excision repair and downstream replication can handle. It acts on psoralen-induced crosslinks and on those arising spontaneously from abasic sites reacting with an opposing base, and it does so without the Fanconi anaemia machinery, so it avoids the double-strand break intermediates and incisions that nuclease-dependent crosslink repair requires. Acting at stalled replication forks, it offers cells a rapid, low-risk first option for crosslink removal, with the Fanconi anaemia route as backup when the lesion resists unhooking.

When a replication fork meets a lesion it cannot copy, such as an abasic site, replication would stall and collapse unless a specialised polymerase takes over. REV1-mediated translesion synthesis is one such bypass route: REV1 acts as a dCMP transferase that inserts a C opposite the damaged template position, and also as a scaffold that recruits the extension step. Monoubiquitinated PCNA, loaded by the replication factor C clamp loader onto RPA-coated DNA, marks the damage site and stimulates REV1 recruitment. Handover then goes to DNA polymerase zeta, whose catalytic subunit REV3L pairs with MAD2L2 (REV7), the subunit that physically binds REV1. Polymerase zeta extends past the lesion with low fidelity and low processivity, so this pathway preserves replication and cell survival at the cost of point mutations, and contributes to damage tolerance and chemotherapy resistance.

When a replication fork meets a damaged base it stalls, and DNA polymerase iota provides one way past the block: translesion synthesis by POLI lets replication continue across lesions that the high-fidelity polymerases cannot copy, trading accuracy for completion of the genome. This tolerance matters because unrescued stalled forks collapse into breaks and cell death, though the same error-prone copying contributes to mutation load. POLI is unusual in favouring Hoogsteen rather than Watson-Crick pairing, flipping template purines to a syn conformation so that adducted or edge-damaged G and A can still be read. Recruitment depends on monoubiquitinated PCNA, loaded by the replication factor C clamp loader onto RPA-coated DNA, together with REV1 as a scaffold. Because POLI extends poorly beyond the inserted nucleotide, polymerase zeta (REV3L with MAD2L2) carries out the extension step.

Single strand annealing is a mutagenic route for repairing DNA double-strand breaks that falls back on direct pairing of repeated sequences rather than faithful copying from a homologous template. It matters because it salvages breaks that cannot be repaired accurately, at the cost of deleting one repeat and everything between them, and because its use reshapes genomes in tumours where accurate recombination is compromised. Breaks first activate ATM and are extensively resected by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex with CtIP and BRCA1-BARD1, then by EXO1 or DNA2 with the BLM and WRN helicases, generating long 3' single-stranded tails that RPA coats and that trigger ATR-TOPBP1-9-1-1 checkpoint signalling. RAD52 heptamers, phosphorylated by ABL1, anneal homologous repeats in opposing tails and simultaneously block invasive RAD51 filament formation, committing the break away from homologous recombination. The ERCC1-ERCC4 endonuclease trims displaced 3' flaps before ligation seals the product.

DNA lesions block the replicative polymerases, and this step is how a stalled fork registers that fact and hands the template to a polymerase that can copy past damage. It matters because a fork arrested at a lesion will collapse into double-strand breaks unless replication is allowed to continue, and because the switch it triggers is inherently mutagenic, shaping the mutation spectra seen in tumours. The clamp loader complex and single-stranded DNA binding protein hold PCNA and polymerase delta or epsilon at the site; when synthesis stalls, RAD18 with its partner ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme UBE2B monoubiquitinates PCNA, weakening replicative polymerase binding and creating a mark read by the ubiquitin-binding motifs of Y-family translesion polymerases. A cullin-RING ligase with DDB1 and DTL also acts on PCNA, while the USP1-WDR48 deubiquitinase reverses the modification, limiting how long error-prone synthesis persists.

Oxidized and alkylated purines are the commonest chemical insults to DNA, and base excision repair begins when a damage-specific glycosylase finds one and cuts it out. Recognition and association of a DNA glycosylase with an affected purine site is that search-and-capture step: the enzyme scans the minor groove, kinks the backbone at the lesion, and flips the damaged base into an active-site pocket where the N-glycosidic bond is cleaved to leave an abasic site for downstream incision and resynthesis. Distinct enzymes cover distinct lesions — 8-oxoguanine by OGG1, adenine mispaired with 8-oxoguanine by MUTYH, alkylpurines by MPG, hydantoins by NEIL3 — and loss of this activity raises mutation rates, with MUTYH deficiency predisposing to colorectal adenomatous polyposis. Because the substrate is chromatin, nucleosomal histones are part of the context, and shelterin components place the same chemistry at telomeres, where oxidative purine damage threatens end protection.

The final stage of global genome nucleotide excision repair restores an intact duplex after a bulky, helix-distorting lesion such as a UV photoproduct has been cut out. Dual incision leaves a gap of roughly 27-30 nucleotides held by replication protein A; the clamp loader RFC deposits PCNA, and DNA polymerase delta, epsilon or the Y-family polymerase kappa copies the undamaged strand to refill it. LIG1 seals the remaining nick during replicative repair, while LIG3 in complex with the scaffold XRCC1 performs ligation in non-cycling cells, giving the step two routes depending on proliferative state. Ubiquitin contributed by the polyubiquitin and ribosomal fusion genes supports PCNA modification and turnover of repair factors. Without this gap-filling and sealing, incision leaves persistent single-strand breaks, and defective nucleotide excision repair underlies xeroderma pigmentosum and its extreme sunlight-induced cancer risk.
